extracted.intended_audience: students preparing for mathematical olympiads (beginner through advanced) and their teachers/coaches
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance, techniques, and problem collections for solving and composing mathematical-olympiad style problems across algebra, geometry, number theory, and combinatorics. Includes worked examples, problem sets, and solution strategies targeted at different skill levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience & problem_selection guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: Select problems of various levels so the book addresses beginning students, advanced competitors, and teachers; group problems by topic and provide both worked examples and proposed problems with complete solutions in a separate solutions part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each section begins with elementary facts, followed by carefully selected problems and extensive discussion of solutions; proposed problems are at the end of each section with complete solutions in Part II. Advice: beginning readers should study solved problems first then attempt proposed problems; advanced readers should seek alternative solutions and generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive symmetric identities via polynomials and determinants
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the polynomial having given numbers as roots or determinant manipulations to obtain symmetric algebraic identities (illustrated by deriving a^3 + b^3 + c^3 − 3abc).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: consider P(X) with roots a,b,c to obtain identity (1.1); expand determinant D to get same expression; several equivalent forms given, e.g. (1.1), (1.2), (1.3). Consequences: if a+b+c=0 then a^3+b^3+c^3=3abc; identity leads to quick proofs of inequalities such as AM–GM for three variables. Technique note: viewing symmetric expressions as polynomials/determinants often yields clean factorizations and insights into equality cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and equality condition
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonzero reals a_i, b_i, (sum a_i^2)(sum b_i^2) ≥ (sum a_i b_i)^2, with equality iff a1/b1 = a2/b2 = ... = an/bn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs given: via nonnegativity of f(x)=sum (a_i - b_i x)^2 and via the lemma a^2/x + b^2/y ≥ (a+b)^2/(x+y). Use the lemma to extend to multiple terms and to prove numerous classical inequalities (many worked problems provided). Always check equality condition (ratios equal) when applying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: a^2/x + b^2/y ≥ (a+b)^2/(x+y) (and its n-term extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a,b,x,y are real and x,y>0, then a^2/x + b^2/y ≥ (a+b)^2/(x+y); equality iff ay = bx. By induction this generalizes to n terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by clearing denominators reduces to (ay − bx)^2 ≥ 0. Use the lemma repeatedly to derive inequalities for three or more pairs, and to transform sums of quotients into a single quotient — a recurring tool in olympiad inequality problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute-value solving strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid exhaustive case-splitting by using algebraic properties of absolute values: |a|=|b| ⇔ a=±b; |ab|=|a||b|; |a+b| ≤ |a|+|b| with equality condition; general bound |±a1 ± ... ± an| ≤ sum |ai|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these identities to simplify equations/inequalities and to reason about equality cases. Examples: solve |2x−1|=|x+3| by converting to ± form rather than splitting all intervals; apply triangle inequality bounds to show impossibility of solutions or to find minima of sums of absolute values (median-type arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter-swap technique for difficult equations
rubrics_metrics.description: When an equation in x with parameter a is hard, sometimes treat a as the unknown and x as parameter to obtain a simpler (often quadratic) equation in a whose discriminant yields structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: transform x^3(x+1)=2(x+a)(x+2a) into a quadratic in a to find parameter values; in other problems introducing an auxiliary parameter simplifies factoring. Use discriminant observations (e.g., it being a perfect square) to deduce solvability and factorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take-the-conjugate technique (for radicals)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compare or simplify expressions containing square roots, form conjugates to rationalize differences or sums and derive tight bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to estimate the difference between arithmetic and geometric means and to evaluate sums/integer parts involving 1/√k. Typical pattern: rewrite √A − √B = (A − B)/(√A + √B) to bound or compute values. Pay attention to domain/sign conditions when applying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convexity and Jensen-type inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f on interval I is convex iff f(λxA + (1−λ)xB) ≤ λf(xA) + (1−λ)f(xB) for λ∈[0,1]; if twice differentiable, f''≥0 characterizes convexity. Convexity implies f(weighted_average) ≤ weighted_average(f), and analogous reversed inequalities for concave functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation: chord lies above graph. Use convexity to prove inequalities by averaging (example: f(x)=x/(s−x) convex leads to a/(b+c)+... ≥ 3/2). Use extensions to multiple points and integrate convexity inequalities to compare integrals (example Problem 1.73). Equality typically when f is linear or arguments coincide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction best-practices and strengthening for the induction step
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard induction is useful, but often one must prove a stronger statement to make the induction step work; identify an invariant or stronger bound that becomes stable when moving from n to n+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to bound a product of (1+1/k^3) by 3, prove the stronger inequality 1+1/1^3...1+1/n^3 ≤ 3 − 1/n, then multiply by the (n+1) term and show the strengthened form holds for n+1. Use induction also to deduce polynomial roots (Problem 1.80) and number-theoretic properties (Fermat's little theorem via binomial coefficients).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model combinatorial selection problems via Hall's marriage lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate selection/existence problems into bipartite matching: treat one class (rows/columns, buses/students, columns/denominations) as 'boys' and the other as 'girls', declare acquaintance when a desirable relation holds, and apply Hall's condition (every k-subset of boys is acquainted with at least k girls) to guarantee a perfect matching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked applications: selecting one card per column to get all denominations, arranging table columns so each row has all numbers, picking students from buses so pairs were different on both rides. Typical proof pattern: for chosen k rows/columns count available distinct partners (using multiplicity bounds) to verify Hall's condition; when violated, deduce structural consequences (used in extremal combinatorics problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check and exploit equality conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying inequalities, always record the equality cases (for Cauchy–Schwarz, triangle inequality, lemma, convexity, etc.) to identify extremal configurations and to verify tightness of bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality often determines structure of extremal examples (e.g., ratios equal in Cauchy–Schwarz, arguments equal in convexity-derived bounds, sign conditions in absolute-value equalities). Use equality characterizations to construct or check problem extremizers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-book structural technique: worked examples then proposed problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize teaching/problem material by first presenting elementary results and illustrative worked problems, then provide a cluster of proposed problems of varying difficulty with full solutions given separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This scaffolding supports self-study: novices study worked examples before attempting proposed problems; instructors can pick suitable problems for training; solutions in a separate part encourage independent attempts.
